entities.name: Yahya al-Shirvani al-Bakubi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Yahya al-Shirvani al-Bakubi (died 1462) was the pivotal 15th-century Sufi master responsible for systematizing the teachings and practices that led to the formal establishment of the Khalwatiyya order, one of the most widespread and influential mystical brotherhoods in the Islamic world, particularly across the Ottoman domains. Originating from the historical region of Shirvan, in present-day Azerbaijan, al-Bakubi synthesized earlier Khalwati traditions, providing the spiritual and organizational framework that would allow the order to flourish, deeply impacting religious life and social structures from Anatolia to the Balkans and Egypt.

Born in Shamakhi, the capital of the Shirvanshahs, Yahya al-Shirvani received his spiritual training through a lineage tracing back to 'Umar al-Khalwati, the eponymous founder of the Khalwatiyya path in the 14th century. Al-Bakubi spent much of his life in Baku, where he established his zawiya (Sufi lodge) and developed a comprehensive curriculum of dhikr (remembrance of God), spiritual exercises, and ascetic practices. His magnum opus, the 'Vird-i Sattar' (Litany of the Veiler), became a foundational text for the order, outlining the specific litanies and meditations central to Khalwatiyya methodology, emphasizing rigorous self-discipline, solitary retreat (khalwa), and intense devotion.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Yahya al-Shirvani al-Bakubi's systematization of the Khalwatiyya order led to its rapid expansion, making it one of the most influential Sufi brotherhoods across the Ottoman Empire for centuries, with millions of adherents and numerous sub-branches.
